definition: Harmful to something or tending to hold it back; also unfriendly or hostile.
example: Cold temperatures are inimical to bacterial growth, so refrigerated food spoils more slowly.
nuance: Unlike hostile, which usually describes people, inimical often describes conditions harmful to something, as in "inimical to growth."
prompt: A gardener explains why her seedlings keep dying along the coast.
options: Salty sea spray is inimical to the tender seedlings planted along her fence.
Her inimical roses, unlike any others in town, win first prize every summer.
Gentle morning sun proved inimical, and the seedlings thrived beneath it.
Her inimical neighbor kindly offered spare compost and a packet of seeds.
reasons: Salt spray damages young plants, so calling it harmful to them fits exactly.
This confuses the word with inimitable, which means impossible to copy.
Something that helps plants thrive is favorable, the reverse of damaging.
A generous, helpful neighbor is friendly, not hostile.

practice.prompt: A manager describes an office where new ideas are always mocked.
options: Constant ridicule of new proposals created a climate inimical to creativity.
Because the meeting room felt so inimical, everyone spoke up freely.
The office had an inimical printer, a model no competitor could ever match.
The inimical conference room seated only four, so meetings felt cozy.
reasons: Mockery discourages fresh ideas, so the climate works against creativity.
A setting that invites open speech is welcoming, the opposite of hostile.
This mixes the word up with inimitable; being unmatched is not being harmful.
The word means harmful or unfriendly; it says nothing about size or coziness.
